The core insight is that all three reject option models—cost-based, bounded-improvement, and bounded-coverage—converge mathematically at the Bayes level, differing only in how they select instances for rejection. This unification implies that any model’s performance can be understood through its alignment with the Bayes classifier and the nature of its selection rule. The bounded-coverage model requires a randomized selection rule because deterministic thresholds may not achieve optimal coverage-risk tradeoff. A key operational element is the notion of a 'proper' uncertainty score, which maintains the correct ordering of conditional risks and allows for principled thresholding. These scores are critical for defining reliable rejection boundaries. The SELE loss framework offers a computationally efficient way to train such scores by optimizing pairwise rankings instead of full risk functions. It introduces a chunking heuristic to manage O(n²) complexity, though this introduces approximation errors.
